claims.text: The as-sintered W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is nanocrystalline.
The as-sintered alloy has a grain size on the order of tens of nanometers.
As-sintered W38Ta36Cr15V11 undergoes radiation-induced precipitation during irradiation.
As-sintered W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening.
Annealing at approximately 1200 °C for about 10 minutes will modestly coarsen the grains.
The proposed anneal will relax and stabilize high-energy grain boundaries.
Moderate grain coarsening and boundary relaxation will reduce the free-energy driving force for solute clustering and precipitation.
Reducing the density of high-energy grain boundaries will reduce the number of preferential nucleation sites for radiation-induced precipitates.
After modest coarsening, the remaining grain boundaries will retain sufficient defect-sink capacity.
Retention of grain-boundary defect-sink capacity will keep irradiation hardening negligible.
At approximately 8 dpa, the annealed alloy will have a lower radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
The annealed alloy's irradiation-defect density will be comparable to or slightly lower than that of the unmodified alloy.
The annealed alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The coarser microstructure will improve suitability for bulk sintering and fabrication without a detrimental tradeoff.
The proposed intervention will remain effective up to approximately 8 dpa at irradiation temperatures of roughly 300–500 °C.
Higher-temperature or longer-duration annealing could over-coarsen the microstructure.
Over-coarsening caused by more severe annealing could impair other mechanical properties.
As-sintered W38Ta36Cr15V11 poses challenges for scale-up to practical bulk forms.

contradictions.description: The intervention is explicitly performed after bulk sintering, yet the predicted outcome says the resulting microstructure will improve or support bulk sintering. A post-sintering treatment cannot improve the already completed sintering step, although it could potentially improve subsequent fabrication or bulk-material stability.
